problemText: A nonrestrictive element is information that a sentence does not need in order to identify what it is talking about. Which sentence contains a nonrestrictive element that is correctly set off with commas?
choices: My best friend Sophia won the spelling bee yesterday.
My best friend, Sophia, won the spelling bee yesterday.
My best friend, Sophia won the spelling bee yesterday.
The student who studied hardest won the spelling bee yesterday.
hints: Use the removal test: cover the name Sophia and see if you can still tell who you are talking about.
When the extra information sits in the middle of a sentence, it needs a matching pair of marks on both sides.

problemText: Jordan has three sisters. One of them is named Maya. Which sentence is punctuated correctly for this situation?
choices: Jordan's sister, Maya, always helps him with homework.
Jordan's sister — Maya — always helps him with homework.
Jordan's sister Maya always helps him with homework.
Jordan's sister, Maya always helps him with homework.
hints: Run the removal test: if Jordan has three sisters, does the name Maya help identify which one?
Restrictive information — information the sentence needs — takes no commas at all.

problemText: The soccer team has only one goalie, and her name is Iris. A student writes: 'Our goalie Iris is the fastest runner on the team.' This sentence is missing punctuation. Which version corrects the mistake?
choices: Our goalie, Iris is the fastest runner on the team.
Our goalie Iris, is the fastest runner on the team.
Our goalie — Iris is the fastest runner on the team.
Our goalie, Iris, is the fastest runner on the team.
hints: The name Iris sits in the middle of the sentence and needs marks on both sides.
A matching pair means you open with one mark and close with the exact same kind of mark.

problemText: There is only one principal at the school, and the student wants to set off extra information with a pair of dashes instead of commas. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: Our principal — Dr. Nakamura — announced a surprise assembly during the morning announcements.
Our principal, Dr. Nakamura — announced a surprise assembly during the morning announcements.
Our principal — Dr. Nakamura, announced a surprise assembly during the morning announcements.
Our principal Dr. Nakamura — announced a surprise assembly during the morning announcements.
hints: Dashes do the same job as commas: they set off nonrestrictive information.
When you use dashes, you must use matching marks — one before the extra information and one after it.

problemText: A student has written two sentences and needs to decide which one is punctuated correctly. The class has only one art teacher. Which sentence correctly reports this fact?
choices: The art teacher who teaches painting and sculpture is Mr. Chen.
The art teacher, who teaches painting and sculpture, is Mr. Chen.
The art teacher, who teaches painting and sculpture is Mr. Chen.
The art teacher who teaches painting and sculpture, is Mr. Chen.
hints: Use the removal test on the clause 'who teaches painting and sculpture.' If there is only one art teacher, can you still tell who is meant without this clause?
When a nonrestrictive clause sits in the middle of a sentence, it needs matching marks — one before and one after — to set it off completely.

problemText: A writer has two different facts to share and wants to punctuate the same sentence two different ways. Fact 1: The restaurant has only one chef. Fact 2: The restaurant has multiple chefs. How should the sentence be punctuated differently for each fact?
choices: For both facts, the sentence should be 'The restaurant's chef Marco creates daily specials' with no commas because the name always identifies which chef.
For both facts, the sentence should be 'The restaurant's chef, Marco, creates daily specials' because a person's name is always set off with commas.
For Fact 1: 'The restaurant's chef, Marco, creates daily specials' (name is extra). For Fact 2: 'The restaurant's chef Marco creates daily specials' (name identifies which chef).
For Fact 1: 'The restaurant's chef Marco creates daily specials' (name is restrictive). For Fact 2: 'The restaurant's chef, Marco, creates daily specials' (name is extra).
hints: The removal test tells you whether information is restrictive or nonrestrictive, and that depends on the fact about how many chefs there are.
The same words in the same order can be punctuated differently depending on what the sentence needs to identify.

problemText: A complete sentence needs three things. Which group of words has all three—a subject, a verb, and a finished thought?
choices: The rain falling hard on the roof while we watched.
Because the rain fell hard on the roof.
Fell hard on the roof during the storm.
The rain fell hard on the roof.
hints: Ask yourself: Who or what is it about? What do they do or are? Does it leave you waiting for more information?
A starter word like because makes the thought unfinished, even if there is a subject and verb.

problemText: Read this group of words: "When the game ended in overtime." Use the three-part test to find what is wrong with it.
choices: It has a subject and verb but is a fragment because a starter word holds it open.
It is missing a verb, which means it cannot form a complete independent clause on its own.
It is a run-on sentence because it incorrectly joins two separate complete thoughts without proper punctuation.
It is missing a subject, so there is no noun to tell who or what the sentence is about.
hints: The word 'when' is a starter word—does it leave you waiting to hear what happened?
Check if there is a subject (the game) and a verb (ended). The problem is not missing those.

problemText: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: After the store closed early we had to go shopping the next day.
After the store closed early, we had to go shopping the next day.
After the store closed early we had to go shopping, the next day.
After the store closed early the store closed, we had to go shopping.
hints: A starter word group at the beginning of a sentence needs to be set off by a comma.
Look for a group of words that begins with a starter word and check if the comma comes in the right place.

problemText: Read this sentence: "The soccer team practiced in the rain, they did not want to miss the scrimmage." Identify the error and choose the best way to fix it.
choices: Move the second clause first: They did not want to miss the scrimmage, the soccer team practiced in the rain.
Use a joining word with a comma: The soccer team practiced in the rain, because they did not want to miss the scrimmage.
Use a period: The soccer team practiced in the rain. They did not want to miss the scrimmage.
Delete the comma: The soccer team practiced in the rain they did not want to miss the scrimmage.
hints: Two complete sentences joined by only a comma is called a comma splice. Check which fix is legal.
Fixes for a comma splice include a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a joining word—but the joining word should show how the ideas connect.

problemText: A student wrote: "Although the recipe called for three eggs we used two instead." Which revision correctly fixes this error without changing the meaning too much?
choices: Although the recipe called for three eggs, we used two instead.
We used two eggs although the recipe called for three eggs.
Although the recipe called for three eggs, we used two instead, which was fine.
Both A and B are correct.
hints: A starter word can come at the beginning or the end. Think about where the comma goes in each case.
Review the rule: starter word at the front gets a comma after it; starter word at the end needs no comma between the two parts.

problemText: A student wrote three versions of the same idea. Read all three and decide which one has NO error at all. "(1) Because I left my homework at school. I had to redo it at home. (2) I left my homework at school I had to redo it at home. (3) Since I left my homework at school, I had to redo it at home."
choices: Version 3 is correct because a starter word is properly attached to a complete sentence with a comma.
Version 2 is correct because it joins two complete thoughts without any extra punctuation marks between them.
Version 1 is correct because it separates the starter-word group from the complete sentence with a period, making two statements.
Version 2 is correct because the two complete sentences are placed side by side to show they are related to each other.
hints: Version 1 has a period between a starter-word group and a complete sentence. Is that legal?
Version 2 joins two complete sentences with no punctuation. Version 3 joins a starter-word group to a complete sentence with proper punctuation. Which one obeys the rules?

problemText: What does it mean when a paragraph has sentence variety? Choose the best answer.
choices: The sentences mix different lengths and starting words instead of repeating the same pattern over and over.
The sentences rely on using fancy words and complicated vocabulary throughout the paragraph to make each sentence sound more interesting and engaging to readers.
The sentences are deliberately written to be consistently long in structure so that the reader has adequate time to fully understand and process each individual idea presented.
The sentences alter the original facts and details presented in order to keep the reader guessing about what the actual message or point of the paragraph truly is.
hints: Look for the answer that describes how sentences are shaped and organized.
Remember: sentence variety changes shape, not meaning or content.

problemText: Read these two sentences from a class newsletter: "The soccer team won the championship. Everyone cheered at the final whistle." These sentences are correct, but the reader has to guess the connection between them. Which revision states the relationship without changing what happened?
choices: The soccer team won the championship, and everyone cheered at the final whistle because it was exciting.
When the soccer team won the championship, everyone cheered at the final whistle.
The soccer team won and everyone cheered, which was the championship at the final whistle.
The soccer team won the championship; everyone cheered very loudly at the final whistle.
hints: Look for a revision that adds a connector word that explains how the two events relate in time.
The connector should show that the cheering happened as a result of the winning.

problemText: Look at this paragraph from a student's journal entry: "Max uploaded his essay. Max submitted it to the teacher. Max waited for feedback." The reader hears a choppy rhythm because of repeated openers. Which revision fixes the repeated pattern without dropping any facts?
choices: Max uploaded a very long essay and submitted it very carefully to the teacher who waited.
Max uploaded his essay. His essay was submitted. Feedback was waited for by Max.
Max uploaded his essay and submitted it to the teacher, then waited for feedback.
Max uploaded his essay, submitted his essay, and waited for feedback from his teacher.
hints: Find the version that combines the first two sentences so the repeated 'Max' opener disappears.
All three facts should still be there—uploading, submitting, and waiting.

problemText: Read this paragraph for a school website: "The rain started at noon. The field became too muddy. The game was postponed until Saturday. The team was disappointed." Every sentence opens with a different word, but the paragraph still sounds choppy. Which revision best improves the rhythm while keeping all facts intact?
choices: The rain started at noon because the field became muddy, the game was postponed until Saturday, and the team was disappointed.
At noon the rain started, and it created muddy conditions so the game moved to Saturday, which made the team feel upset.
The rain started. The field became muddy. The game postponed. The team disappointed.
The rain started at noon, making the field too muddy. The game was postponed until Saturday, and the team was disappointed.
hints: Look for a revision that combines sentences that are closely related and adds a connector to state a relationship.
The best fix will create a mix of shorter and longer sentences instead of four sentences of similar length.

problemText: A student wrote this for a class blog: "The art supplies arrived. We opened the boxes. The brushes were high quality. The paint colors were vivid." The repeated opener 'The' appears in three sentences in a row, and some relationships are left unstated. Which revision removes the repeated opener AND adds a connector that states a relationship?
choices: The art supplies arrived, so we opened the boxes and discovered the high-quality brushes and vivid paint colors.
The art supplies arrived and we opened the boxes. The brushes were high quality and the paint colors were vivid.
When the art supplies arrived, we opened the boxes. The brushes were high quality, and the paint colors were vivid.
The art supplies arrived. We opened the boxes. The brushes were high quality. The paint colors were vivid.
hints: The best fix should eliminate the repeated 'The' opener at the start of multiple sentences in a row.
Look for a version that adds a connector like 'so' to show how one action led to a discovery.

problemText: A student is revising this paragraph for a class magazine: "Emma researched her topic for three hours. Emma took detailed notes. Emma organized her information by topic. Emma created an outline before she wrote her draft." The student tries two fixes. Fix 1 changes it to: "Emma researched her topic for three hours and took detailed notes. She organized her information by topic and created an outline before she wrote her draft." Fix 2 changes it to: "Emma spent a lot of time researching her topic carefully. She took some detailed notes. She organized her information by topic. She created an outline before she wrote her draft." Which fix actually solves a real problem you can point at in the words, and why?
choices: Fix 2, because it uses longer, fancier words like 'spent' and 'carefully' to sound more interesting.
Fix 1, because it removes the repeated 'Emma' opener from the beginning of sentences in a row.
Neither fix solves a real problem; both just rearrange the same four facts without changing the rhythm.
Fix 2, because it changes the subject from Emma to 'She,' which makes the paragraph sound less repetitive.
hints: Remember: a real fix either removes a repeated opening word or adds a connector that states a relationship.
Changing words to sound ancier is not the same as fixing the repetitive pattern.

problemText: A piece of writing establishes one register—either formal or informal—and should keep it consistent throughout. Which of the following is a signal that a sentence is written in a formal register?
choices: It contains a personal opinion stated with exaggeration, such as 'basically the best ever.'
It includes an exclamation point and everyday language that sounds like a friend talking.
It uses precise vocabulary and formal transitions rather than slang or casual filler words.
It uses casual asides and filler words like 'anyway' or 'you know' to connect ideas.
hints: Look for the choice that describes careful, professional word choice.
Formal register uses precise wording, not slang or casual filler.

problemText: Read this school announcement: 'The district is implementing a new lunch schedule starting next month. All students will receive a menu one week before the change takes effect. Tbh the new schedule is gonna be pretty lit and everyone will love it. Food service will post updates on the school website.' Which sentence breaks the formal, informative tone of the rest of the announcement, and why?
choices: The sentence about the menu breaks it because it uses formal language like 'receive' rather than the casual tone established in the rest of the announcement.
The sentence about implementing a new lunch schedule breaks it because it states the district's main policy at the beginning instead of saving it for the conclusion of the announcement.
The sentence about food service updates breaks it because it uses 'school website' to communicate information rather than employing other methods such as printed notices or parent emails.
The sentence with 'Tbh the new schedule is gonna be pretty lit' breaks it because it uses slang, casual abbreviations, and personal opinion instead of formal wording.
hints: Look for the choice that identifies exactly what makes one sentence different from the others in word choice and tone.
Compare the wording in each sentence—which one uses slang and casual filler that the others do not?

problemText: Read this personal email to a friend: 'I got my test score back today and I was so pumped because I actually passed. The studying we did together really paid off, and honestly it felt amazing. The academic rigor of the assessment instrument necessitated extensive preparation and cognitive engagement. We should definitely study together again before the next one.' Which sentence does not match the warm, casual tone the writer establishes in the other sentences?
choices: The sentence with 'The academic rigor of the assessment instrument...' because it uses stiff, formal vocabulary instead of everyday words.
The sentence about studying together, because it uses the phrase 'study together' when the writer should have used a more casual expression like 'team up' or 'work it out.'
The sentence about getting the test score back, because it fails to specify whether the test was administered during class time or as a take-home assignment.
The sentence about the score paying off, because it employs a metaphor rather than stating plainly that the preparation directly improved the test result.
hints: The lapse might be a grammatically correct sentence, but its register does not match.
Which sentence uses formal, precise vocabulary that sounds completely different from the friendly, excited tone of the rest?

problemText: A student wrote this paragraph for a history class report: 'The invention of the printing press in the fifteenth century transformed how information spread throughout Europe. Scholars could now reproduce texts quickly instead of copying them by hand, which saved enormous amounts of time. Ngl, it was literally the coolest thing that ever happened to books and learning, I'm not gonna lie. This innovation allowed ideas to reach wider audiences and fueled the growth of the scientific revolution.' To fix the register inconsistency, which of the following rewrites best replaces the sentence that breaks the formal tone while keeping the same basic information?
choices: Books were super important back then, and people really cared about spreading ideas around because the printing press made it easier to do so.
The widespread distribution of printed texts accelerated the exchange of knowledge and contributed significantly to intellectual advancement.
It was really cool how books changed and everyone thought the printing press was awesome for learning and sharing information.
People used the printing press a lot because they thought it was better than writing things out by hand and it helped spread their ideas.
hints: The replacement must use formal, precise wording that matches the rest of the report.
Look for a choice that conveys the importance and impact of the printing press without slang, exaggeration, or casual filler.

problemText: A student is writing a thank-you note to their grandmother for a birthday gift. The note includes these sentences: 'Thank you so much for the amazing sweater you sent me. I wore it to school on Monday and all my friends were asking where I got it. Furthermore, the aforementioned garment is manufactured from premium textile materials of exceptional durability. I really appreciate how thoughtful you always are.' The student wants to maintain a warm, grateful tone throughout. Which statement correctly identifies the problem sentence and explains why it needs to be changed?
choices: The sentence about wearing it to school is the problem because personal anecdotes are inappropriate in thank-you notes and the focus should remain entirely on expressing gratitude without describing specific occasions.

The sentence about friends asking is the problem because it shifts attention away from the grandmother's generosity and makes the letter seem more interested in peer validation than in genuine thanks.
The sentence about manufacturing and textiles is the problem because its stiff, formal vocabulary breaks the warm, personal tone established by the other sentences.
The sentence about appreciation is the problem because it appears after sentences that already convey gratitude and therefore becomes redundant and weakens the overall message.
hints: The lapse is a sentence that has no grammar errors but does not sound like a warm, personal conversation.
Which sentence uses technical, formal language that clashes with the friendly, grateful tone of the rest of the note?

problemText: A student is revising an article for the school newspaper about an upcoming sports event. The draft reads: 'The girls' soccer team is competing in the district tournament next Saturday. Fans are invited to attend and cheer on our athletes. The squad demonstrated exceptional athletic prowess and tactical proficiency during their preliminary matches. Tickets cost five dollars and may be purchased at the door. The team's hard work will definitely make them a strong competitor.' The student knows one sentence breaks the established register but is unsure whether to rewrite it in formal language or informal language. Based on the register of the surrounding sentences, which revision strategy should the student use, and which sentence needs fixing?
choices: Rewrite the sentence about ticket cost in formal language, because practical information should always sound professional.
Rewrite the sentence about the team's hard work in formal language, because that sentence sounds too casual compared to the others.
Rewrite the sentence about athletic prowess in informal language, because formal vocabulary is never appropriate for a school newspaper.
Rewrite the sentence about athletic prowess in informal language, because the rest of the article uses casual, conversational wording.
hints: First, identify which register most of the sentences in the article use by comparing them to each other.
Notice that the majority of sentences use straightforward, accessible wording—then find the one sentence that stands out with formal jargon.
